profile.reading:
This building, mapped as NTT Chicago CH4, sits at 1200 Arlington Heights Road, Itasca, IL 60143, part of the same broader Itasca, DuPage County campus as NTT's CH1 (255 Pierce Rd) and CH2 (275 Pierce Rd) buildings, though on a separate street. NTT does not publish an individual facility page for CH4, so this entry's address is drawn from public geocoded property data rather than an operator-confirmed page, and specific square footage or MW figures for this building could not be independently confirmed this session; that gap is stated plainly rather than estimated. NTT's own materials describe its combined Itasca-area campus, which the operator says includes four buildings (CH1 through CH4), as exceeding 200 megawatts of critical IT load in total; CH1 and CH2 alone account for 72 of those megawatts per NTT's own per-building pages, implying CH3 and CH4 together supply the balance.

Illinois's data center tax incentive program has become a flashpoint for state energy policy. Governor JB Pritzker announced on June 5, 2026 a temporary suspension of new awards under the state's Data Center Investment Program, citing grid strain; ComEd's CEO stated the program had added roughly $12 a month to the average residential bill over the prior four years. From 2020 through 2024, 27 data centers statewide received more than $983 million in tax incentives under the program.

NTT's US Global Data Centers footprint spans seven named campuses in total: Ashburn, Virginia at 224 megawatts; Chicago, Illinois at more than 200 megawatts; Dallas, Texas at 160 megawatts; Hillsboro, Oregon at 126 megawatts; Phoenix, Arizona at 240 megawatts; and a combined Sacramento/Santa Clara, California figure of 68 megawatts, totaling roughly 1,118 megawatts or more of disclosed US capacity, per the operator's own locations page. The US business operates under the NTT DATA Global Data Centers Americas name, the successor brand to RagingWire Data Centers, now under Japan's NTT DATA Group and parent Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation, a Tokyo Stock Exchange-listed company not subject to SEC 10-K filing requirements.

reading.body:
CH4's published IT capacity is 36 MW. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 36 MW of IT load is roughly 900 racks; at 10 kW per rack, a common colocation average, the same power supports roughly 3,600 racks. The assumption you make about rack density changes the answer by a factor of four, so the published megawatt figure is the only hard number to reason from.

No published specifications for cooling headroom, raised-floor area, or power redundancy tier appear on the source page, so no further architectural claims can be derived. Whether CH4 supports dense GPU workloads depends on cooling and power delivery specifications that are not published. NTT holds no certifications listed in the data provided, so no certification-based qualification statement can be made.

CH4 ranks second among the six Illinois facilities on this site that publish a megawatt figure, accounting for roughly 15 percent of the 236 MW of published IT capacity across that group. Illinois has 44 facilities mapped in OpenStreetMap, but only 6 publish a capacity figure, meaning the 236 MW total almost certainly understates the state's real installed base by a wide margin. For a reader sizing AI infrastructure, 36 MW is a meaningful block of power in a state where the median published facility figure is far smaller, but it is not hyperscale territory by current AI campus standards, where single campuses are now announced at hundreds of megawatts.

The data used here carries unresolved uncertainty. CH4's address and megawatt figure appear to have been inherited from a source page for a different facility, CH1, and could not be independently verified this session because CH4's own facility page no longer publishes and CH4 does not appear on NTT's current Chicago locations overview.
